title: Onboard Training and the Standard of Competence under STCW Chapter III, and the Chief Engineer's Role
canonical_question: Explain the salient factors for onboard training and the standard of competence required under chapter III of STCW as amended. Underline the specific roles a Chief Engineer must perform towards the satisfactory training of engine-room personnel, and state the criteria for evaluating competence in onboard training.

limb_of.limb_label: B. Onboard training and the standard of competence under STCW chapter III, the Chief Engineer's role, and the criteria for evaluating competence

sibling_limbs.limb_label: The major changes the Manila amendments made for the engine department

present_day_examinable_core: UNCHANGED_CORE, reframed only to drop the obsolete 'existing versus amended chapter III' comparison. The printed limb asks three things and they must be answered as three: what makes onboard training count under STCW, what a Chief Engineer specifically has to DO about it, and what the criteria for evaluating competence actually are. The third is the part that is nearly always missed, and it has a precise answer - the competence tables in the STCW Code are laid out in four columns, and 'criteria for evaluating competence' is the name of one of them.

recommended_exam_depth.note: MIW's recommendation for the second of two limbs. The sittings that evidence this family print a paper total only, with no per-question or per-limb split, so no mark here is inherited from any examiner's paper.

understand_first: There is one structural fact that unlocks this whole limb, and a candidate who knows it will out-score one who does not by a wide margin. The competence tables in part A of the STCW Code are written in FOUR COLUMNS: the competence itself; the knowledge, understanding and proficiency that underpins it; the methods for demonstrating competence; and the CRITERIA FOR EVALUATING COMPETENCE. So when the examiner asks for 'the standard of competence' and then for 'the criteria for evaluating competence', those are not two ways of saying the same thing - they are two named columns of the same table, and the second is the column that says what an acceptable performance looks like. Name the four columns and the rest of the answer writes itself. The second thing to hold onto is what makes onboard training count at all: seagoing service earns a certificate only when it is APPROVED, STRUCTURED, DOCUMENTED and SUPERVISED BY A QUALIFIED PERSON. Time served is not training. A cadet who has spent twelve months on board being useful has not necessarily completed a day of approved onboard training, and the Chief Engineer is the person who determines which of those two things happened.

blocks.h: Three headed parts, because the examiner asked three questions

blocks.p: Head them Onboard training and the standard of competence, The Chief Engineer's specific roles, and The criteria for evaluating competence. The third part is the discriminator, so give it its own section and its own examples rather than folding it into the first.

ul: Open with the four columns of the STCW Code competence table. It frames everything and it takes two lines.
Say what makes onboard training approved - a documented programme, a training record book, a qualified supervisor and assessor, tasks tied to real work, and records the Administration can audit.

Name chapter III by regulation - III/1 for the officer in charge of a watch, III/2 for management level, III/4 and III/5 for ratings - and note that each has its own seagoing service and onboard training requirement.

Make the Chief Engineer's roles concrete and personal. 'Ensure training is carried out' is worth little; 'plan the trainee's tasks against the record book, allocate a qualified supervising officer, sign only what I have seen, and report the gap to the Company' is worth a lot.
Give real criteria, in the Code's own idiom - observed performance judged against a stated standard - and say plainly that attendance and time served are NOT criteria.
Bring in the ISM Code at the end. Onboard training is also a Company duty and is auditable, which is why it has to leave a record.

blocks.h: 1. How chapter III is built, and where onboard training sits in it

blocks.p: Chapter III of the Convention sets the mandatory minimum requirements for the engine department. Each certificate has its own regulation, and each regulation requires three things together: approved education and training, approved seagoing service, and the standard of competence specified in the corresponding section of part A of the STCW Code.

rows: III/1
Officer in charge of an engineering watch

Requires approved seagoing service which includes a specified period of engine-room watchkeeping duties under the supervision of a qualified engineer officer, and, where the route is a cadetship, an approved onboard training programme documented in a training record book
III/2
Chief engineer officer and second engineer officer
Management level. Competence at this level includes the management of personnel, of training and of the safety management system - so the holder is not only trained, he is the trainer
III/3
Chief and second engineer officer on ships below a specified propulsion power
Same structure at a reduced power band
III/4 and III/5
Rating forming part of a watch, and able seafarer engine
Both rest on approved seagoing service together with training - onboard or ashore - and on the corresponding competence standard
III/6 and III/7
Electro-technical officer and electro-technical rating
Introduced by the 2010 Manila amendments, and built on the same three-legged structure

blocks.p: What makes onboard training count. Sea time by itself earns nothing. Approved onboard training has five salient features, and they are the marks in the first part of this question:

ol: An approved, structured programme. The training scheme is approved by the Administration and is planned rather than opportunistic - a defined set of tasks and objectives covering the competences the certificate requires.

A training record book. The tasks are recorded as they are completed, with the date and the signature of the officer who supervised and verified each one. The record book is the documentary bridge between what happened in the engine room and what the Administration will accept.

Qualified supervision and assessment. The person supervising the training, and the person assessing it, must themselves be appropriately qualified for the task or competence concerned and must have an appreciation of the training programme. A senior hand who is excellent at the job is not automatically a qualified assessor.

Real work, properly sequenced. Training tasks are tied to the ship's actual operation and maintenance, planned so the trainee builds from supervised observation, through assisted work, to unsupervised performance - and always within the safety of the plant and of the trainee.

Quality standards and auditability. The whole arrangement sits inside a quality standards system monitored by the Administration, and inside the Company's safety management system, so that it can be evaluated rather than asserted.

blocks.h: 2. The standard of competence, and the four columns

blocks.p: Competence in STCW is not knowledge. It is the demonstrated ability to perform a defined task to a defined standard, and the Code expresses each one in a table of four columns:

rows: 1. Competence
The task itself, stated as an ability
Operate main and auxiliary machinery and associated control systems
2. Knowledge, understanding and proficiency
What must be known and understood to underpin the ability
Operational principles, preparation for and starting of machinery, safe and effective operating limits, and the associated procedures
3. Methods for demonstrating competence
How the ability may be shown and by what evidence
Approved in-service experience, approved training-ship experience, approved simulator or laboratory training, or assessment of practical performance on board
4. Criteria for evaluating competence
What an ACCEPTABLE performance looks like - the standard the assessor judges against

That the machinery is operated in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions and the ship's procedures, that parameters are kept within safe limits, and that departures are detected and corrected

blocks.p: Because the fourth column exists, the Convention does not allow competence to be certified on the strength of a course attended or a period served. It requires a judgement about performance against a stated standard, made by a qualified person, and recorded. That is the whole architecture, and it is the answer to the third part of this question.

blocks.h: 3. The specific roles a Chief Engineer must perform

blocks.p: This part should be written in the first person and made concrete. A Chief Engineer's duty here is not general encouragement; it is a set of identifiable acts.

ul: Own the programme on board. Read the training record book and the approved programme on joining, establish what each trainee still needs, and turn that into a plan for the voyage rather than reacting to whatever breaks.

Allocate qualified supervision. Nominate for each trainee an officer who is competent in the task and who understands the programme, and make that allocation known. Do not leave supervision to whoever happens to be on watch.

Integrate training into real work. Plan planned-maintenance jobs, surveys, bunkering, tank entry, dry-dock work and drills so that trainees are deliberately included - the opportunity is what the ship is doing anyway, and it is lost if nobody plans it.

Ensure familiarisation before duty. Under the ISM Code and STCW, no one takes up a duty until they are familiar with the ship's arrangements, equipment and procedures for that duty. This is a safety obligation and it comes before any training objective.

Assess, and sign only what I have seen or had verified. The signature in a record book is a professional attestation of competence. Signing a page to keep a cadet's paperwork moving is a false statement that will be relied upon by an Administration, and it is the failure mode a Chief Engineer must refuse.

Give feedback and appraise. Debrief tasks, tell the trainee where the performance fell short of the criteria and what to do about it, and complete honest appraisals - the value of an appraisal is entirely in its honesty.

Instruct in safety and in limits. Permits, isolation and lock-out, enclosed-space entry, hot work, electrical safety including high voltage, and the discipline of stopping a job. A trainee's first competence is knowing when not to proceed.

Keep the records and report the gaps. Maintain the training records, hours of rest and drill records, and where the programme cannot be completed - the ship's trade does not present the task, or there is no qualified assessor on board - report that to the Company as a deficiency rather than closing the book. That report is the mechanism by which the system corrects itself.

Manage the department so that training is possible. Realistic workload, protected rest and a no-blame reporting culture. Nobody learns anything useful in a department that is behind on everything and afraid to admit a mistake.

Set the standard personally. Watchkeeping discipline, record-keeping, tidiness of work, use of the correct tool and the correct procedure. Trainees copy what the Chief Engineer tolerates, not what he says.

blocks.h: 4. The criteria for evaluating competence in onboard training

blocks.p: Stated generally first, then illustrated. The criteria are always of the same shape: an observable performance, judged against a defined external standard, in circumstances that are representative of the real duty.

ul: The performance conforms to the applicable standard - the manufacturer's instructions, the ship's procedures, the safety management system, and the relevant convention requirement. Not to the assessor's personal preference.
Operating parameters are kept within safe and effective limits, and the trainee can state what those limits are and why.
Deviations are detected early and correctly interpreted, and the response is appropriate and timely. Recognising an abnormal condition is a competence in its own right.
The correct priority is chosen under pressure - safety of life, then the ship, then the environment, then the plant - and help is called at the right point rather than too late.
Communication is effective: orders and reports are given, received, and acknowledged unambiguously in the working language, and the trainee reports what they have actually done.
Safety precautions are complete before work starts - permit, isolation, ventilation, testing, personal protective equipment - and are verified rather than assumed.
The task is completed to a serviceable standard, with clearances, settings and tests recorded and the work handed back properly.
The performance is repeatable, in more than one instance and, where the duty demands it, without supervision.

blocks.p: And the criteria that are not criteria. Time served, attendance at a course, willingness, seniority, or the fact that nothing went wrong. Say this explicitly - it is the sentence that shows the examiner you have understood the fourth column rather than memorised it.

How the assessment is actually made. Direct observation of practical performance on board is the primary method, supported by oral questioning to test the underpinning knowledge, by examination of the trainee's records and reports, by simulator or workshop evidence where the ship cannot present the task, and by the record-book verification that ties each item back to a named qualified officer on a named date.

blocks.h: 5. Where this joins the Company's obligations

blocks.p: Onboard training is not only a Convention matter. The ISM Code requires the Company to establish procedures to identify any training which may be required in support of the safety management system and to ensure it is provided; to ensure new personnel and personnel transferred to new assignments are properly familiarised; and to verify, review and evaluate the whole arrangement. So the training record book, the familiarisation checklist, the drill record and the Chief Engineer's training plan are auditable documents - examined at internal audit, at the ISM verification behind the Safety Management Certificate, and at port State control. That is the practical reason the records matter as much as the teaching does.

Three parts were asked and three parts are given, in the examiner's order. The four-column structure of the Code's competence tables is the intellectual centre of the answer and it does two jobs at once: it answers 'the standard of competence' and it makes the 'criteria for evaluating competence' a precise question with a precise answer instead of an invitation to generalise. Very few candidates name the four columns; almost none say which of them the examiner is asking about.

ul: Answering 'criteria for evaluating competence' with methods of assessment. Those are column 3. Column 4 is what an acceptable performance looks like. Give both, labelled, and the distinction earns the mark on its own.
Treating sea time as training. Approved onboard training is structured, documented, supervised by a qualified person and auditable. Twelve useful months is not twelve months of training.

Writing the Chief Engineer's role as a policy statement. 'Ensure adequate training is provided' could have been written by someone who has never been to sea. Name the acts: read the record book, allocate a qualified supervisor, plan tasks against the programme, sign only what was seen, debrief against the criteria, and report the gap to the Company.

blocks.h: What this answer deliberately does not claim

ul: No table numbers, section paragraph numbers or quoted Code wording. The chapter III regulation numbers are given because they are stable and well established. Beyond that, MIW does not hold the STCW Code under licence, so competences and criteria are described in their own idiom rather than quoted, and the four column headings are named as the structure of the tables - which is documented and stable - without any claim to reproduce a particular table's contents.

No periods of seagoing service in months. The requirement that approved seagoing service include a specified period of supervised engine-room watchkeeping is stated; the figure is not, because the qualifying periods differ between certificates and between training routes and are in each case set by the regulation and by the Administration. A single number here would be quoted in an exam as though it applied to every route.

No claim that the training record book is a Convention-named document for every certificate. It is the normal instrument of an approved onboard training programme and is required where that route is used; the answer places it there rather than presenting it as universal.

blocks.h: How this limb sits beside its sibling

blocks.p: This family is owned limb by limb because it holds two genuinely independent examinable concepts, and the governed QI join QIJ-0005 is the objective evidence for that: the stem of this limb is, on its own, another recurrence family in MIW's corpus. CA-EM-0007 answers the other limb - what the Manila amendments changed for the engine department. Reading both is useful; each was reviewed on its own evidence and neither verifies the other.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Chapter III certificates each need three things together: approved education and training, approved seagoing service, and the standard of competence in part A of the Code. Onboard training counts only if it is an approved structured programme, recorded in a training record book, supervised and assessed by a qualified person, tied to real work, and auditable under a quality standards system. The competence tables have FOUR columns - competence; knowledge, understanding and proficiency; methods for demonstrating; and criteria for evaluating. The criteria are an observable performance judged against the manufacturer's instructions, ship's procedures and the SMS, with parameters kept in limits, deviations detected, correct priorities, effective communication, complete precautions, a serviceable result, and repeatability. Time served and attendance are NOT criteria. The Chief Engineer plans it, allocates qualified supervision, familiarises before duty, signs only what he has seen, debriefs against the criteria, keeps the records and reports the gaps to the Company.

critical_numbers: Four - the number of columns in each STCW Code competence table, and the reason 'standard of competence' and 'criteria for evaluating competence' are two different questions
Three - the legs every chapter III certificate stands on: approved education and training, approved seagoing service, and the standard of competence

No qualifying period in months is quoted, on purpose: the periods of approved seagoing service and of supervised engine-room watchkeeping differ between certificates and training routes and are set by the regulation and the Administration - see the study guide
quick_revision.critical_regulation: STCW 1978 as amended, chapter III - regulation III/1 for the officer in charge of an engineering watch, III/2 for chief and second engineer officer at management level, III/3 for the reduced propulsion-power band, III/4 and III/5 for ratings, III/6 and III/7 for electro-technical officer and rating - each requiring approved education and training, approved seagoing service and the standard of competence in the corresponding section of part A of the STCW Code. Chapter I for quality standards and for the qualification of instructors, supervisors and assessors. The ISM Code for the Company's duties to identify and provide training, to familiarise personnel before they take up duty, and to verify, review and evaluate.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering the 'criteria for evaluating competence' with the METHODS of assessment - observation, oral questioning, simulator. Those are the third column. The fourth column is the standard an acceptable performance is judged against, and it is what the examiner asked for.

authority_sources.source: STCW 1978 as amended, chapter III - mandatory minimum requirements for the engine department: regulations III/1, III/2, III/3, III/4, III/5, III/6 and III/7, each requiring approved education and training, approved seagoing service and the standard of competence specified in the corresponding section of part A of the STCW Code; and the requirement that approved seagoing service for the officer in charge of an engineering watch include supervised engine-room watchkeeping, documented in a training record book where an approved onboard training programme is the route
authority_sources.checked: Confirmed in force as at 24 August 2026, and confirmed to be the Manila text with the transitional arrangements ended on 1 January 2017, so no earlier standard runs in parallel. The regulation numbers and the three-legged structure of each certificate were established. MIW does not hold the STCW Code under licence: competences and criteria are therefore described in their own idiom and NOT quoted, no table or paragraph reference is asserted, and no qualifying period in months is stated, because those periods differ between certificates and routes.

authority_sources.source: STCW Code part A - the four-column structure of the tables of competence: competence; knowledge, understanding and proficiency; methods for demonstrating competence; and criteria for evaluating competence
authority_sources.checked: The four column headings are the documented and stable structure of every competence table in part A of the Code, and are relied on here as structure rather than as content. Confirmed as at 24 August 2026. The engine-room illustrations given against each column in the answer are MIW's own worked examples, written to show what each column does; they are NOT quotations from any particular table, and the answer does not present them as such.

authority_sources.source: STCW chapter I and the corresponding Code sections - quality standards systems monitored by the Administration, and the requirement that those conducting training, supervision and assessment be appropriately qualified for the task or competence concerned and have an appreciation of the training programme
authority_sources.checked: Confirmed in force as at 24 August 2026. Cited for the two propositions the answer actually makes: that approved training sits inside an auditable quality system, and that competence in a job does not by itself qualify a person to assess it.

authority_sources.source: ISM Code - the Company's duty to establish procedures to identify training required in support of the safety management system and ensure it is provided, to ensure new personnel and personnel transferred to new assignments are properly familiarised with their duties before taking them up, and to verify, review and evaluate the system
authority_sources.checked: Read at source and confirmed in force and unamended in substance as at 24 August 2026. Cited to establish that onboard training records are auditable documents rather than internal paperwork, which is the practical reason the record-keeping half of a Chief Engineer's duty matters.

authority_sources.source: Onboard training and assessment practice - sequencing from supervised observation through assisted work to unsupervised performance; the professional meaning of a verifying signature in a training record book; debriefing against stated criteria; and reporting an uncompletable programme item to the Company as a deficiency rather than closing it
authority_sources.checked: Settled training practice with no governing instrument, declared as such. It is the operational content of the Chief Engineer's role section, and no instrument is cited for it. The one point worth flagging is that the refusal to sign an unverified record-book entry is presented here as professional obligation and not as a Convention requirement, which is the honest attribution.

not_yet_in_force: The comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code is in progress at IMO and NOTHING from it is adopted or in force. It bears directly on this answer, because training and assessment methods are within its scope, and it is the event that will require this entry to be revisited. A candidate may say the review is under way; a candidate may not present any of its content as a requirement.
superseded_framework: The comparison between 'the existing chapter III of STCW 95' and 'the amended chapter III', which the printed family wording invites, has no present-day content: the Manila amendments entered into force on 1 January 2012 and the transitional arrangements ended on 1 January 2017. This limb is therefore answered against chapter III as it now stands, and the obsolete comparison is dealt with in the sibling limb CA-EM-0007 where it belongs.

review_record.notes: Reviewed against the question and the cited authority. FIVE checks. SCOPE, and this is a limb entry so the sibling test comes first: the entry does not answer CA-EM-0007. The Manila amendments appear only where chapter III's own structure requires them - regulations III/6 and III/7 exist because of them - and the obsolete 'existing versus amended' comparison is explicitly handed to the sibling under superseded_framework rather than being answered twice. Clean. STRUCTURE AGAINST THE PRINTED TASK: three things were asked - salient factors for onboard training and the standard of competence, the Chief Engineer's specific roles, and the criteria for evaluating competence - and the answer has a headed section for each, in that order. The third is given its own section, which is the correct weighting because it is the part the printed wording asks for by name and the part almost every answer folds into the first. THE LOAD-BEARING CLAIM was checked hardest: that the Code's competence tables have four columns, the fourth being 'criteria for evaluating competence'. This is the intellectual centre of the answer and if it were wrong the answer would be worthless, so it was verified as the documented structure of part A of the Code, and - importantly - the entry relies on it as STRUCTURE while stating in terms that the engine-room examples given against each column are MIW's own worked illustrations and not quotations from any table. That is the distinction between using a stable framework and pretending to hold a licensed text, and the entry gets it right in both the authority record and the study guide. OVER-CLAIM CHECK: no qualifying period in months anywhere, with the reason stated - the periods differ between certificates and routes. No table number. No quoted Code wording. The refusal to sign an unverified record-book entry is labelled professional obligation rather than Convention requirement. Each of those is a place the answer could have inflated itself and does not. EXAM UTILITY: the Chief Engineer section is written as ten identifiable acts rather than as policy, and the answer states explicitly what is NOT a criterion - time served, attendance, seniority, nothing having gone wrong - which is the sentence that demonstrates understanding rather than recall. PASS.

The family was resolved limb by limb rather than whole because the governed QI join QIJ-0005 records QIF-EM-0068 as a WHOLE_VS_LIMB_RELATION of QIF-EM-0061 at 0.9667 containment - this limb's stem is, on its own, a separate recurrence family - which is objective evidence of two independently examinable concepts rather than a bracket split. The reuse order was applied first: the nearest solved candidates in MIW's corpus answer the human element in the STCW Code with the IMO fatigue guidance, and competence against performance with automation, and neither answers onboard training, the competence tables or the criteria for evaluating competence.
version_history.authority: STCW 1978 as amended, chapter III and chapter I, and the four-column structure of the part A competence tables; ISM Code read at source for the Company's training, familiarisation and review duties; onboard training and assessment practice as settled professional practice.

next_review_trigger: Re-review when the comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code reaches its adoption meeting, since training and assessment methods are within its scope and it is the single event most likely to change this answer. Also re-review if MIW acquires the STCW Code text under licence, which would allow the competence-table illustrations to be replaced by properly cited content and would remove the largest declared limitation on this entry; or if MIW solves a past paper that sets onboard training and the criteria for evaluating competence directly, in which case the relationship between that sitting-anchored answer and this one must be adjudicated rather than assumed.
